explanations.answer: There is no more bread in the city
explanations.explanation: That's the reason, baker. Ebed-melech says Jeremiah will starve “…for there is no more bread in the city.” (Jeremiah 38:9). Down in the mud with no one bringing food, I think the clock was already running. The famine Jeremiah talked about was already pressing on Jerusalem.

explanations.answer: The officials took away his food
explanations.explanation: That sounds believable, friend, but the text never says it. Ebed-melech says Jeremiah will starve “…for there is no more bread in the city.” (Jeremiah 38:9). So the problem is the whole city running out. Nobody mentions anyone taking his food.

That's right, baker. They pulled him up with the ropes, “And Jeremiah remained in the courtyard of the guard.” (Jeremiah 38:13). Out of the mud is a big win, but he is still there. I'm glad the pit part is over.

explanations.answer: The king will surely put him to death
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Jeremiah answers King Zedekiah, “If I tell you, you will surely put me to death.” (Jeremiah 38:15). He's just been pulled out of a mud pit, so I think I'd hesitate too. And he's being asked to hide nothing.

explanations.answer: The king will throw him back in the cistern
explanations.explanation: That's an easy fear to picture after the mud, friend. But Jeremiah says something else: “If I tell you, you will surely put me to death.” (Jeremiah 38:15). He isn't worried about the pit. He's worried about his life.

explanations.answer: The king will send him off to Babylon
explanations.explanation: Babylon is on everybody's mind in this chapter, but it isn't what Jeremiah says here. He tells King Zedekiah, “If I tell you, you will surely put me to death.” (Jeremiah 38:15). Nothing about a trip. Just a serious fear for his life.

explanations.answer: He will not kill him or hand him over
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Zedekiah swears, “As surely as the LORD lives, who has given us this life, I will not kill you, nor will I deliver you into the hands of these men who are seeking your life.” (Jeremiah 38:16). He does it secretly, with the LORD's name behind it. That's a big promise.

explanations.answer: He will send him away from the city
explanations.explanation: Getting out of town would help, friend, but that isn't the promise. Zedekiah swears, “…I will not kill you, nor will I deliver you into the hands of these men who are seeking your life.” (Jeremiah 38:16). It's about keeping him alive and not handing him over. Moving him out of the city isn't part of it.

explanations.answer: He will do whatever the LORD says
explanations.explanation: That would be a different promise, and a good one, baker. But the oath Zedekiah swears is about Jeremiah: “…I will not kill you, nor will I deliver you into the hands of these men who are seeking your life.” (Jeremiah 38:16). He swears it by the LORD's name. He does not promise to do what the LORD says.

I see where you're going, baker, but the word is different. Jeremiah says the LORD's promise is, “…you will live, this city will not be burned down, and you and your household will survive.” (Jeremiah 38:17). It's about the city not burning. Nothing here talks about emptying it.

That's right, baker. If he refuses to surrender, Jeremiah says the LORD's word is, “…you yourself will not escape their grasp.” (Jeremiah 38:18). The city would also be burned down. Zedekiah has two paths in front of him.

explanations.answer: The Jews who have deserted to the Chaldeans
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Zedekiah says, “I am afraid of the Jews who have deserted to the Chaldeans, for the Chaldeans may deliver me into their hands to abuse me.” (Jeremiah 38:19). I think that fear is real to him. It's the reason he gives for not surrendering.

explanations.answer: The prophets who spoke against Jeremiah
explanations.explanation: That's a fair guess in a chapter full of people against Jeremiah, friend. explanations.answer: He asked not to be sent back to Jonathan's house to die
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Zedekiah tells Jeremiah to say, “I was presenting to the king my petition that he not return me to the house of Jonathan to die there.” (Jeremiah 38:26). That's the story Jeremiah is given for the officials. Nobody mentioned this house before, but it's a handy line.

explanations.answer: He came to report to the king on the officials' plans
explanations.explanation: That's a tricky answer, friend, and it would stir up the officials. But it isn't what the king tells him to say. Zedekiah says to answer, “I was presenting to the king my petition that he not return me to the house of Jonathan to die there.” (Jeremiah 38:26). It's a request for himself.

explanations.answer: He came to pray for the king and the people of the city

Zedekiah tells him to say, “I was presenting to the king my petition that he not return me to the house of Jonathan to die there.” (Jeremiah 38:26). It's a petition about Jeremiah himself. explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. They said no more to him, “…for no one had overheard the conversation.” (Jeremiah 38:27). Jeremiah gave them the exact words the king had commanded him to say. Without a witness, the officials had nothing to push on.

explanations.answer: The king ordered them to leave him alone

explanations.answer: They feared what the people might do
